title: Bringing Change In The Anti-Food, Food Industry — Why Farmtheory Exists
body_markdown:
#### The dream: everybody was food waste fighting! 🥕


#### **Bringing a fresh perspective to the table 🌱**


We love food. We love being in the thick of Bangalore’s B2B food supply ecosystem. But for all our reputation as being a creative back-end arm of those who create a plethora of cuisines and culinary delights, we realise our industry is strangely old-school, keen on maintaining the status quo rather than embracing the new.


The food service and processing industry, comprising restaurants, food processing units, cloud kitchens, caterers and various food-related businesses, is currently witnessing a wave of transformation. Rapid urbanisation, changing consumer preferences, and a rising population have fuelled the growth of restaurants, cafes, fast-food chains, and fine dining establishments across the city.


With this rise, addressing food waste has become paramount. India loses approximately 40% of its food production, with a significant portion occurring during post-harvest, processing, and distribution due to inefficient supply chains.


#### Out with the old and in with the new? 🌅


The world certainly doesn’t need another supply chain company. But what we believe it does need is a serious re-imagination of the food supply chain and experience — both for the growers and makers of food.


The growers i.e. farmers deserve better market access, more transparency and favourable partners that treat their entire harvest with the same care and affection as they do.


The makers i.e. chefs and production heads deserve people who catch their pulse. Who understand the complexities and hassles of running a kitchen and go way above the functional layer of just selling them quality ingredients and offering a reliable service.


The food supply chain, on the whole, deserves people who care about people and beyond that, about food loss and the giant cloud of uncertainty that looms over our future.


#### Embracing a better and inclusive food system 🤗


With Farmtheory, we have ideas that we believe can fundamentally alter what being a food supply partner means. Ideas around tackling inequity, bridging the gap between growers and makers, questioning grading standards, eliminating middle people and commissions, grappling with the lack of a humane approach in a human-centric industry, etc.


Now some of these ideas are actually quite boring. For starters, we believe one of the easiest ways for serious disruption in the supply of fnv (fruits and vegetables) may be as simple as having a serious conversation about the unrealistic cosmetic standards for fnv established by traditional users in our industry. Calling out their tendency to prioritise certain aesthetic qualities over other important factors, such as nutritional value, taste, ethical sourcing and reducing food loss.


For this, we’ve eliminated the usage of terms such as A-grade, B-grade and C-grade at our organisation. So how do we distinguish and grade produce? The fruits and vegetables from a farmer’s harvest that meet conventional aesthetic standards, including preferred colour, size, and shape — we call them Traditional fnv to remove their earlier status of superiority. (A-grade)


The fruits and vegetables from a farmer’s harvest that exhibit variations in colour, size, or shape, that do not conform to conventional aesthetic standards and may be big, small, misshaped, or have surface-level blemishes — we call them Freeform fnv to remove their earlier status of inferiority. (B-grade, ugly, misfit, odd, unsized, etc.)


Further, the fruits and vegetables from a farmer’s harvest that cannot be used because they’re unsafe for human consumption or too small to have monetary value, we call them fnv loss to restore their dignity and respect while raising awareness about food loss. (C-grade, dump, rejection, etc.)


Our focus is on achieving a high freeform fnv density at our organisation’s core. Why?


Because acceptance of freeform means acceptance of a farmer’s harvest based on quality, nutrition and taste rather than looks. And that leads to the greater good of saving good food.


#### Moving towards a just food industry 👣


The inequity around which our industry has been built is another reality that bites us. When we see the on-ground gender disparity in commercial kitchens, when we listen to farmers talking about being cheated with fraudulent seeds and pesticides, when we see freeform vegetables only being bought for staff food by ‘traditional users’ exclusively because their commercial value is lower — it bothers us.


This inequity not only hampers the progress of our industry but also perpetuates social and economic disparities. To us, it’s imperative that we work towards a more equitable and inclusive food supply ecosystem that benefits all stakeholders. As a start, we are dedicated to building an inclusive company with a culture that values honesty, ethics and compassion.


#### Now, why should all this matter to our growers and makers? 👩‍🍳 👨‍🌾


Well, it’s only natural that the residual benefits of all of this will flow directly into our work with them. At Ft, we want to give our growers and makers the best food supply experience they’ve ever had. When a farmer or a kitchen chooses us, we want them to know that we’re committed to being trailblazers who put the freshest, most ethically sourced produce on the table. How we operate internally is going to play a huge role in making that happen.


We all know perfectly well what needs to improve in the imperfect food supply business: we just plan to execute it more consciously. And at the end of all of this, we just want to do good to our planet! 🌏
